stories.topic: The Bad Hair Day That Became a Show Opener
stories.summary: Amit woke up with the dilemma of whether to wet his hair (since wetting it would force him to dry-comb-uncomb it back into a 'natural scruffy look'). He attempted it, was told by his cameraman Vaishnav that his hair was a mess, tried various fixes with the team, and finally just gave up and decided to be comfortable on camera regardless. He notes 'some of you are lucky enough to be able to listen only to the audio version.'
stories.insight: A small but recurring template Amit returns to: comfort with looking imperfect on camera is part of being a serious public thinker. The work matters; the styling doesn't. He has 'a face for audio' — and now, he discovers, 'a head for audio' too.

stories.topic: The Pakistani Press Outraged That India Is Their 'Most Favoured Nation'
stories.summary: In trade-treaty language, MFN ('most favoured nation') just means 'whatever tariff cut we negotiate with anyone, we apply to all our partners.' Pakistan's press has periodically erupted with horror that, technically, Pakistan treats India as 'most favoured.' Hawks demand it be repealed, not realising the term is a piece of trade-treaty plumbing, not a diplomatic ranking.
stories.insight: A perfect example of how technical jargon, parsed through political lenses, becomes political ammunition. The same word means 'standard rule' to economists and 'betrayal of the nation' to nationalists — and in the gap between those two readings, real policy gets made.

stories.topic: Rare Earths — China's Pollution Got Them a Global Monopoly
stories.summary: Rare earths aren't actually rare; the deposits exist all over the world. But extracting them is painful, polluting work, and lax Chinese environmental regulation made it cheap to do there. Over decades that handed China a global monopoly. In 2011 they cut off rare earth sales to Japan; in 2025 they announced a blockage on sales to the United States. The threat is the leverage.
stories.insight: A monopoly built not on innovation but on willingness to absorb a cost (pollution) that others wouldn't. The lesson for global supply chains: any country willing to bear an externality others avoid will end up holding a chokehold on the rest of the world.

stories.topic: The 80% API Vulnerability of Indian Pharma
stories.summary: India runs one of the world's great generic-drugs industries — but the active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) that go into those drugs are 80% sourced from China. In an ideal world this would be a private-to-private transaction. But Chinese firms are indirectly controlled by the Communist Party. So in any negotiation — say, over Ladakh — the Chinese could threaten in private rooms to cut off API exports, forcing India to choose between a strategic concession and the collapse of one of its successful export industries.
stories.insight: Specialisation is the engine of comparative advantage but also the engine of vulnerability. When the country you depend on is a 'revisionist power' rather than a status-quo friend (UK, Germany), the same supply chain that makes you efficient becomes the lever they use to coerce you.

stories.topic: Apple Filling Planes With iPhones to Beat the Tariff Clock
stories.summary: When Trump's China tariffs were announced, Apple started filling jumbo cargo planes 'to the gills' with iPhones, shipping them out of Madras to America before the tariffs landed. The image captures the absurdity of the moment — one of the world's most sophisticated companies racing physical goods around the planet to dodge an arbitrary policy lever pulled in Washington.
stories.insight: Uncertainty has its own enormous cost. Even before tariffs hit, the response of every globalised firm is panic-rerouting and contingency planning — capital being burned not on production but on insurance against capricious policy.

stories.topic: Watching Adolescence in Business Class — Weeping in the Aisle
stories.summary: Flying back from Spain in business class, Amit watched the four-episode British series Adolescence on his iPad. By the middle of episode four — each shot in a single take — he was weeping openly. Fellow passengers in nearby business-class seats glanced at him with looks of 'you are one of the luckiest people in the world, what is going on?' He notes you can have all the champagne you want; he doesn't drink, on flights or otherwise.
stories.insight: The premise that great popular art can blow you apart in public is the whole reason Amit pushes back at Ajay's pessimism about contemporary culture. If you let yourself engage, you find masterpieces in the mainstream — and weeping in business class is what real engagement with art looks like.

stories.topic: Kemi Badenoch Grilled For Not Watching Netflix
stories.summary: On a British breakfast show, two anchors grilled Kemi Badenoch — leader of the Conservative opposition — over the moral failing of not having watched Adolescence. Badenoch said she'd been talking to actual parents and kids and didn't need to watch Netflix to engage with the issue: 'To understand what is wrong with hospitals, I don't need to watch Casualty.' One anchor called the show 'a great documentary' (it is fiction). They appeared not to have watched it themselves.
stories.insight: A cautionary tale about culture-as-political-litmus-test. The same show that is genuinely a masterpiece can be weaponised by people who haven't seen it as a moral cudgel against people who haven't seen it. Engaging with the world directly beats engaging with the world via prestige TV — but the latter is easier to perform.

stories.topic: The 'Olive Branch' India Quietly Extended Trump
stories.summary: When Trump's tariff regime began, the Indian government quietly proactively withdrew the so-called 'Google tax' — a 6% equalisation levy on overseas digital companies. Ajay always thought it was a dumb idea anyway. The withdrawal was a signal: 'Yeah, we get it, these kinds of things are not considered good behaviour in the new world of trade.'
stories.insight: A small, mature move that cost India nothing it valued and bought it goodwill from a capricious negotiating partner. Diplomacy at its best is recognising which of your own bad policies you can painlessly repeal as 'concessions.'

recommendations.item: Adolescence
recommendations.creator: Stephen Graham, Jack Thorne
recommendations.context: A four-part Netflix series, each episode shot in a single take, about a boy alleged to have committed a crime.
recommendations.reason: Amit was 'blown away' by it on a flight back from Spain — weeping by the middle of episode four. Two reasons it amazes him: the level of craft is a new pinnacle in filmmaking, and that something this good is also wildly popular — a counter-example to Ajay's pessimism about popular culture. Forget what's been written about it on social media (right and left have made it a stupid identity-politics football); it's not political, it's about the human condition.

recommendations.item: Anora
recommendations.creator: Sean Baker
recommendations.context: The 2024 Best Picture Oscar winner.
recommendations.reason: Amit cites it as further evidence we are in 'a golden age of cinema.' The last 20-25 minutes are 'just so masterful, so masterful. Just brilliant.' Two decades ago the Oscar often went to mainstream pap; now genuinely great films are winning.

recommendations.item: Perfect Days
recommendations.creator: Wim Wenders
recommendations.context: Wim Wenders' meditative film about a Tokyo toilet cleaner.
recommendations.reason: Listed among Amit's exhortations to Ajay to engage with contemporary cinema rather than dismissing popular culture from a distance — part of his 'we live in a golden age' argument.

recommendations.item: Dekalog
recommendations.creator: Krzysztof Kieslowski
recommendations.context: A Polish television series of ten films, made for TV before 'web series' existed.
recommendations.reason: Amit's prior pinnacle of long-form audiovisual storytelling. He'd 'never seen anything like it' — a web series before the web, which set the template for what shows like The Wire and now Adolescence have built on.

recommendations.item: The Wire
recommendations.creator: David Simon
recommendations.context: The HBO series.
recommendations.reason: For Amit, the show that finally brought a 'novelistic ethic' to the audiovisual medium — things unfolding organically, with the sweep and economies-of-scale of a great novel. A bridge between Dekalog and Adolescence in his canon of long-form masterpieces.

recommendations.item: Want Free Trade? May I Introduce You to the Tariff
recommendations.creator: Robert Lighthizer
recommendations.context: Lighthizer's New York Times opinion piece (6 February 2025) summarising the Trumpist case against the post-WTO trade order.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it 'the best article I read' from the American Right on tariffs. Multiple people sent it to him asking how he would respond, which forced him to think carefully. Contains the cleanest articulation of how non-tariff barriers, hidden subsidies, currency manipulation, and predatory tax systems have hollowed out the WTO framework — even where you reject Lighthizer's prescriptions, he frames the diagnosis sharply.

recommendations.item: Where Did the Bombay Club Go Wrong?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A 2009 Ajay Shah piece on the Indian industrialists who lobbied for state protection post-1991.
recommendations.reason: Counterpoint to the rosy view that Indian industry was always pro-liberalisation. The Bombay Club showed how local capitalists can choose 'rule a small protected pond' over 'compete in a big global market' — the wrong choice that better entrepreneurial confidence would have rejected.

recommendations.item: Trade Liberalisation: Looking Beyond the WTO
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A 2009 Ajay Shah essay arguing for trade liberalisation beyond the WTO framework.
recommendations.reason: Background reading for the episode's argument that the WTO model has run out of steam and what comes next must look more like deep integration treaties (TPP-style) than another GATT round.

recommendations.item: Egregious Indian Protectionism Against Trade in Services
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A 2012 Ajay Shah piece on Indian non-tariff barriers in services trade.
recommendations.reason: Direct evidence for the episode's central economic claim: services are now 67% of world GDP and the GATT/WTO never opened them up. India's own protectionism in services is one example of why a TPP-style 'WTO 2.0' is needed.

recommendations.item: India: An Agricultural Trade Powerhouse
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A 2019 Ajay Shah piece arguing India should embrace agricultural trade.
recommendations.reason: Counter to the GATT-era assumption that 'agriculture is history' — for India, where 40-60% of the population still works in agriculture, free trade in agriculture is in the national interest, even if the developed world abandoned it.

recommendations.item: India's Supply Chain Vulnerability With Chinese APIs
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah and others
recommendations.context: A 2021 paper on Indian pharma's dependence on Chinese active pharmaceutical ingredients.
recommendations.reason: The detailed treatment of the API vulnerability story Ajay tells in this episode — and the original location of the 'wise, uncorrupt, sophisticated, minimally-state-intervention' design framework for reducing the dependency.

recommendations.item: The Case for Trade Barriers Against Chinese Imports
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A 2024 Patnaik-Shah piece arguing — carefully — for selective trade barriers against China.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's most direct articulation of the four-part criticism of pure free trade with revisionist powers: military conflict, economic statecraft, scale-economy gaming, and macroeconomic spillovers. He treads in 'this dangerous territory with extreme caution' — but argues the case must be made.

recommendations.item: Envisioning an India-US Free Trade Agreement
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A 2024 Business Standard article written after the December 2024 emerging markets conference.
recommendations.reason: The episode's punchline. Ajay reports a 'fascinating consensus from the American side' that one of the few politically feasible US trade deals is a deep FTA with India. Trump's tariffs make it more salient, not less — Trump can claim victory; India can secure cheap goods.

recommendations.item: Two Divergent Measures
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A 2025 Ajay Shah piece on the uncertainty shock from Trump's policy regime.
recommendations.reason: Companion to the episode's argument that the bigger story is not narrowly tariffs — it is the global uncertainty shock as every large firm rethinks its production geography in an environment where Trump has power until November 2026 and possibly beyond.

recommendations.item: Implications of US Tariffs
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A 2025 Ajay Shah piece spelling out the consequences of the Trump tariff regime.
recommendations.reason: The detailed economic case that the destruction of existing global supply chains is 'tantamount to throwing bombs on present production facilities' — a direct reduction in the world's capital stock.

recommendations.item: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's earlier comprehensive episode on Indian agriculture.
recommendations.reason: Background for the GATT-era 'abandon agriculture' decision and why it didn't fit India — where 40-60% of the population still works in agriculture, versus 5% in the developed world.

recommendations.item: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Episode 40, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's clean-energy episode covering polysilicon and solar panels.
recommendations.reason: Source of the polycrystalline-silicon-and-solar-panels case study Ajay returns to — Chinese subsidised scale-economy gaming has hollowed out the global solar manufacturing industry.

recommendations.item: How to Do Development (Episode 57, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on the nature of economic development.
recommendations.reason: The grounding for Ajay's claim that 'economic development is not a manual; it's learning by doing.' Once a manufacturing knowledge base is yanked away, it takes years to recreate — which is why Chinese supply-chain dominance is hard to undo.

recommendations.item: The Reformers (Episode 28, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE's episode on the Indian reformers of 1991.
recommendations.reason: Amit closes by saying further unilateral tariff liberalisation 'would please the soul of Manmohan Singh' and the other reformers covered in this earlier episode — a callback to the 1991 moment as the template for what India should now do again.

recommendations.item: Andrew Doyle's tweet on Kemi Badenoch's grilling
recommendations.creator: Andrew Doyle
recommendations.context: Andrew Doyle's tweet pointing to the British breakfast-show interview where Kemi Badenoch was harangued for not having watched Adolescence.
recommendations.reason: Source of Amit's anecdote about cultural shows being weaponised politically. Doyle is described by Amit as 'a great free speech thinker' — the tweet itself is the entry-point for the longer point about the absurdity of treating Netflix as a political litmus test.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policymaking.
recommendations.reason: The standing reference for the analytical frame Ajay uses throughout — 'wise and sensible' state intervention, recognition of state-capacity limits, and the case for minimally invasive policy. Cited as the source of the design framework for reducing strategic vulnerabilities like the API dependency without falling into crony capitalism.

recommendations.item: Life Lessons
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An online course taught by Amit and Ajay.
recommendations.reason: Plugged at the top of the episode — the show's ongoing educational project alongside the podcast.

core_ideas.concept: War vs. Trade — The Two Fundamental Paradigms
core_ideas.explanation: There are only two ways for a society to advance: the martial outlook (grab land, take resources) and the shopkeeper's outlook (trade your way to whatever you need). Trade is positive-sum, war is negative-sum. The two paradigms always coexist; the question is which dominates. Smoot-Hawley (1930) didn't just cause an economic disaster — it set the conditions for World War II. The Japanese invasion of Manchuria (1931), the Italian conquest of Ethiopia (1935), German Lebensraum doctrine — every one of those was a martial response to being shut out of an international trade system. Every push toward autarky is a push toward war. The choice isn't policy preference; it's civilisational.
core_ideas.quote: Every push in favor of autarchy is taking us closer to a military and a martial outlook and a way to make progress by killing people.

core_ideas.concept: RTAA 1934 and the Magic of Most-Favoured-Nation
core_ideas.explanation: The Reciprocal Tariff Agreements Act of 1934 — passed under Roosevelt after Hoover lost over Smoot-Hawley — gave the US president authority to negotiate tariff cuts with other countries on a reciprocal basis. It also baked in MFN: any tariff cut negotiated bilaterally was extended to all trading partners. This was the genius of the design: bilateral reciprocity provided the political bargain (you cut, we cut), while MFN sustained a structural bias toward continual tariff reduction. Without MFN, you'd get a patchwork of treaty-by-treaty tariffs and trade-diversion games. With it, every cut spreads everywhere.
core_ideas.quote: Every tariff cut may be negotiated one, but it will be for all.

core_ideas.concept: Why GATT Worked — The Three Foundations
core_ideas.explanation: GATT (1945) succeeded because three pieces aligned. (1) Agriculture had already faded in the developed world (5% of workforce), so they jettisoned it from negotiations rather than fight rice-farmer lobbies. (2) Trade was synonymous with manufacturing — no services, no fibre optics — and the global corporations that made manufactured goods were aligned with liberalisation as a lobbying force. (3) The West had military and development-aid leverage to coax holdouts (India, Mozambique, South Africa) into the system. By 2025, all three pieces have come apart: services are 67% of world GDP and untouched by treaties; corporations have lost interest because their game is now services; and the West has retreated from the leverage that used to break holdouts.

core_ideas.concept: Why GATT Stopped Working — The Three Failures
core_ideas.explanation: Same three pieces, three failures. (1) Services — now 67-71% of GDP — are barely covered, so the legacy treaty system is fighting yesterday's battle (manufacturing tariffs) when the real game is services liberalisation. (2) Multinationals lost interest because they got what they wanted on goods and the system never upskilled to fight for services. (3) The West retreated post-Cold-War: smaller military budgets, smaller foreign-policy budgets, smaller aid budgets — and therefore no leverage when one 'dinky country' vetoes a multilateral round. Critically, India has long been one of the most important spoilers in trade liberalisation rounds — entirely against India's own interest.

core_ideas.concept: The Privilege of Trade Is Imports, Not Exports
core_ideas.explanation: The standard mercantilist intuition — exports are great, imports are bad — is exactly upside down. The real privilege of international trade is that you get to buy cheap things from overseas. Subsidised Chinese solar panels are a gift, not a threat. India makes software, sells it abroad, uses the revenue to buy cheap solar panels — that is the basal case. Cheaper goods raise consumer welfare, the freed money flows back into other employment, and the economy is better off. When someone subsidises your imports, take the subsidy with open arms.
core_ideas.quote: How nice that the Chinese government is subsidising those solar panels. That is our basal case.

core_ideas.concept: The Four Disquiets of Modern Free Trade
core_ideas.explanation: Even committed free-traders like Ajay now hold four reluctant doubts. (1) Military conflict — should Germany sell Russia precision machine tools that go into T-90 tanks? Dual-use goods make this messy. The military-industrial base depends on a civilian engineering base; you can't isolate one. (2) Economic statecraft — supply-chain specialisation creates chokeholds (Chinese APIs, rare earths) that revisionist states can use as coercion tools, including in private threats. (3) Scale-economy gaming — China systematically violated WTO rules by hidden subsidies (cheap credit, expropriated land, subsidised electricity), achieved global monopolies in things like polysilicon, and is now positioned for monopoly recoupment that will be very slow to undo. (4) Macroeconomic spillovers — when a $19-trillion-GDP country responds to its own debt overhang by flooding the world with cheap goods, every other country absorbs the unemployment shock.

core_ideas.concept: Recoupment vs. Contestability — The Two Theories of Monopoly
core_ideas.explanation: The classical theory of monopoly says: a firm subsidises low prices to kill rivals (the build-up phase), then raises prices once it owns the market (the recoupment phase). Amit's empirical objection: in the real world, without state coercion, recoupment never happens. Amazon, Jio, cell-phone carriers — none of them ever raised prices above their pre-monopoly level. The economics textbooks are simply wrong on this. Ajay's reframe: the right question isn't 'is there a monopoly?' but 'how contestable is the industry?' If Amazon raised prices on hand towels, Myntra would step in tomorrow — low entry barriers. But complex manufacturing is the opposite: Chinese rare-earth or polysilicon recoupment would take other countries 5-10 years to challenge, because the supply-chain knowledge isn't transferable. So the recoupment fear is empirically idle in software/retail and uncomfortably real in heavy manufacturing.
core_ideas.quote: It is a series rubbish. Give me the concrete example, you're giving me the theory.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's organising distinction. Status-quo powers (UK, Germany, Japan) are committed to the existing liberal international order — they wouldn't weaponise trade against you. Revisionist powers (China, Russia, Iran, North Korea) view the current order as illegitimate and treat all economic relationships as instruments of state power. Free trade theory implicitly assumes status-quo trading partners. Once a revisionist power becomes systemically large (China at $19T GDP), the same dependency that delivers gains-from-trade hands them coercive leverage. The asymmetry isn't in the economics — it's in whether your trading partner has internal democratic checks and balances against expropriating their own private sector for state ends.

Ajay's careful distinction, against Lighthizer's blurring. (1) Level-playing-field standards — Europe's GDPR, the phytosanitary rules for grapes — apply equally to local and foreign companies and are the legitimate democratic right of voters. Indian grape exporters must just figure out how to comply if they want the European market. (2) Non-level-playing-field rules — Indian data localisation requirements that force cloud data to physically reside in India — are explicit non-tariff barriers that block foreign competition while paying lip service to WTO rules. The first kind is fine; the second is the actual problem. Critics like Lighthizer often blur them, treating any regulation as a 'subsidy' or 'unfair practice' — which is mumbo-jumbo that needs questioning.
core_ideas.quote: It is the appropriate trade-off of the Indian voter and the Indian industry for the Indian state to find a reasonable balance between economic prosperity and pollution.

core_ideas.explanation: Trump's tariff calculations were built on a fundamental confusion: that a country's bilateral trade deficit with another country is somehow a measure of that country's unfair barriers. Amit's reductio: 'I have a bilateral trade deficit with my local egg shop because I only buy eggs from him and he never buys the services of an uh prominent podcaster.' Trade balances are net flows of comparative advantage; bilateral deficits with individual partners are a feature of specialisation, not evidence of cheating. The 'tariff math' Trump's team produced — calculating tariffs from bilateral trade deficits — is not bad arithmetic so much as a bad model dressed up as arithmetic.
core_ideas.quote: Just imagine they hired the one Indian who doesn't know maths.

core_ideas.concept: The Uncertainty Shock as Capital Destruction
core_ideas.explanation: The biggest cost of the Trump tariff regime is not the tariffs themselves but the uncertainty they create. Every globalised firm — Apple, every multinational — built supply chains over decades, optimised for production-here, distribution-there. Throwing this into doubt is 'tantamount to throwing bombs on present production facilities.' It is a direct reduction in the world's capital stock. Two dimensions: (1) prospective — every firm planning a new factory now has an unanswerable headache about where to put it; (2) legacy — every firm with an existing global configuration is now scrambling to rewire. Both cost money. Until November 2026 and possibly beyond, the uncertainty itself is the macroeconomic shock.

core_ideas.concept: TPP-Style Deep Integration as the Way Forward
core_ideas.explanation: The WTO model — 100+ countries, simple rules (no tariffs, no export subsidies, MFN), one veto stops everything — is exhausted. The forward path is 'deep integration' treaties: a smaller core of willing rich countries plus India hammers out a comprehensive agreement covering services, non-tariff barriers, hidden subsidies, IP, currency manipulation, military exports, environmental practices — with enough specificity that no one can game it. Architecture is open: Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Pakistan can join later, but only on take-it-or-leave-it terms. The Trans-Pacific Partnership was conceived as exactly this kind of WTO 2.0; the world needs the next attempt. Subtract the United States and China from the picture — both have lost the capacity to lead it — and you're left with OECD plus India.

The Trump moment is, paradoxically, the best opportunity India has had since 1991. A deep India-US Free Trade Agreement is the rare proposal both sides could accept: Trump can claim victory by listing fifteen ways India 'cheated' that he forced open; India gets cheaper goods, cheaper cars (Amit calculates a 30% reduction), and a stronger relationship with the world's most important country. Once that's done, do it with the UK, EU, Japan. Amit's stronger version: skip the bilateral deals, just unilaterally remove all tariffs and non-tariff barriers. 'We've put rocks on our own coastline; remove the rocks.' The 1991 reformers — Manmohan Singh and others — would weep with joy.
core_ideas.quote: My dream is that we have no tariffs at all. Forget trade agreements. Unilaterally remove all tariffs.

core_ideas.concept: The Bombay Club Choice — Two Kinds of Industrialist
core_ideas.explanation: When liberalisation is on the table, an industrialist has two responses available. (1) 'Protect us — keep tariffs up, keep us shielded — we will rule a small fixed pond.' (2) 'Open the market — give us scale — we will compete and become great companies.' The Bombay Club, lobbying for state protection in 1990s India, made the first choice. Industrialists in the developed world consistently made the second. Which choice an economy's capitalists make is a measure of their entrepreneurial confidence — and a leading indicator of where the economy will end up.

Amit pauses mid-debate to define the term: to steelman an argument is to present it so well that the person making it could have said it that way themselves. The opposite is strawmanning — misrepresenting the argument to make it easy to attack. The discipline matters because, in any honest disagreement, you should be able to articulate your opponent's case at least as strongly as they would. Amit then steelmans Ajay's case against Chinese trade behaviour before stating his own dissent — the model practice.

core_ideas.concept: We Live in a Golden Age of Cinema
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's recurring counter to the 'culture is dumbing down' narrative. Adolescence is a new pinnacle in filmmaking and is also wildly popular. Anora — the 2024 Best Picture Oscar — would have been art-house twenty years ago; the Oscars used to go to 'mainstream pap.' World cinema, festival cinema, mainstream prestige TV — all of it is in a golden age, if you actually engage. The criticism that great culture is gone usually comes from people who don't engage with what's being made now. Amit's offer to Ajay: 'I will be your guide through popular culture.'

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on his hair crisis: 'When I started The Seen and the Unseen, people would ask me why an audio podcast, and I would say I have a face for audio. I have realized today, today I have realized I also have a head for audio.'
Amit on bilateral trade deficits: 'I have a bilateral trade deficit with my local egg shop because I only buy eggs from him and he never buys the services of a prominent podcaster.'

Ajay on Trump's tariff math, after a Twitter wag pointed out the relevant Trump official had an Indian name: 'Just imagine they hired the one Indian who doesn't know maths. Apologies to whoever that is. If you're watching this, learn some math, bro, while you're working for Trump.'

Amit, on Ajay's neologistic flourish that the Trump shock is 'an adverse global macroeconomic shock': 'You used a lot of jargon there. What you actually meant to say is that the shit has hit the fan.'
Ajay, on calling the USSR collapse one of the great achievements of human history: 'You mean to say the collapse was one of the great achievements — in case anyone misunderstands — not the USSR.'

Amit, slightly horrified at the irony of his weeping fellow business-class passengers: 'You are one of the luckiest people ever, the fuck can you... It's supposed to be emotional? Yeah, you can have all the champagne you want.'
Ajay, dryly describing Donald Trump throughout: 'Into this came a stable genius called Donald Trump.'

Amit on the Indian political compass: 'In India, of course, we have no conception of right or left. All parties are what we would call left wing on economics, right wing on society — which is exactly the opposite of what it should be, because they're both anti-freedom.'
Amit on the Trump vs Bernie convergence: 'Trump and Bernie Sanders in fact are so similar in their anti-free-trade thinking...'

Smoot-Hawley Tariffs (1930) — the disastrous American tariff law that triggered global retaliation, contracted world trade by 66%, and is repeatedly invoked here as the model for how trade wars set the conditions for shooting wars.

Lebensraum — German doctrine of 'living space,' i.e. the martial-territorial alternative to a trading order. Cited alongside the Japanese invasion of Manchuria (1931) and Italian conquest of Ethiopia (1935) as consequences of the autarkic moment after Smoot-Hawley.

John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White — the two architects of the post-1944 international economic order (IMF, World Bank, Marshall Plan, GATT). Ajay invokes Keynes as the kind of dreamer the world now lacks: 'Sadly we don't have a John Maynard Keynes today.'
'In the long run, Keynes is dead' — Amit's pun on Keynes's famous 'In the long run we are all dead,' deployed as a beat in the Keynes-as-missing-architect riff.
Robert Lucas's 'we have conquered the business cycle' — invoked here against the wreckage of macroeconomic stability now produced by a single capricious trade actor.

Frederick List and Thomas Mun — the canonical 16th-19th century mercantilists/economic-nationalists Ajay names as the lineage of the Trump position: a recurring 'standard trope' that pure free traders have always had to argue against.
'The arsenal of democracy' — the Roosevelt-era phrase for the United States' manufacturing base that won World War II. Ajay's point: that arsenal is now in China, not America.
Wolf-warrior diplomacy — the Chinese diplomatic style Ajay names as evidence of the revisionist character of the contemporary CCP.
'A century of humiliation' — the standard Chinese nationalist framing of the period from the Opium Wars to 1949, invoked here as the resentment fuel for the revisionist stance.
Joan Robinson's 'rocks on our own coastline' — the line Amit quotes for unilateral tariff reform. To put up tariffs is to throw rocks on your own coast; to remove them is to clear your own harbour.

Francis Fukuyama's 'The End of History' — invoked as the high-water mark of post-1989 complacency. Amit notes the original essay had a question mark, and Fukuyama meant 'end' in the means/end sense, not 'over.'

The Washington Consensus — coined around the same era, capturing the elite confidence that the development formula was solved (A, B, C, and you'll be fine). The episode argues the popular opposition was always there; the elites just didn't take it seriously.
The Great Illusion (1909) — Norman Angell's pre-WWI book arguing that economic interdependence had made war obsolete. Repeatedly invoked as the cautionary tale against complacency.

Martin Amis on bad criticism: 'The worst kind of criticism is when you criticize an author for not writing the book you want.' Amit deploys this against vogue criticisms of Adolescence for not centering the female victim.
Casualty (the BBC medical drama) — Kemi Badenoch's deflection of the Adolescence grilling: 'To understand what is wrong with hospitals, I don't need to watch Casualty.'

Sayadri Farms in Nashik — the farmer-connected organisation Amit and Ajay visited; the source of the example that Europe demands no pesticides for two months before grape harvest, a level-playing-field standard rather than a non-tariff barrier.
'Papnaki Dilki Bata, sir' — Amit's mock-portentous Hindi-film aside cueing Ajay to elaborate the 'India's opportunity' chapter.
